text:
Houston, We've Had a Problem

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Apollo 13 was meant to be the third lunar landing, and by then the public had begun to treat such flights as routine. Television networks skipped live coverage of the crew's broadcasts. Few people watching that launch could have guessed that within three days the mission would become one of the most gripping struggles for survival in the history of spaceflight.

The commander was Jim Lovell, a veteran of three earlier flights who had already circled the Moon on Apollo 8. Fred Haise, a rookie, was to pilot the lunar module. The command module pilot was supposed to be Ken Mattingly, but days before launch doctors worried that he had been exposed to German measles, and he was replaced by his backup, Jack Swigert. Swigert had trained only briefly with his new crewmates. He was a bachelor, quick on his feet, and he had not expected to fly at all.

The spacecraft was a pair of linked vehicles. The command module, named Odyssey, was the crew's cabin and the only part built to survive the fiery return through the atmosphere. Attached behind it was a service module holding the engine, the oxygen, the water and the fuel cells that made electricity. A third vehicle, the lunar module Aquarius, rode folded inside the rocket's upper stage until the crew pulled it free and docked with it on the way out. The first two days passed smoothly.

The seeds of disaster had been planted years earlier. One of the two oxygen tanks in the service module had been installed in an earlier spacecraft and dropped slightly when it was lifted out for repairs. Later, during a ground test, technicians struggled to drain it, so they ran heaters on it for hours at a voltage higher than its thermostat switches were designed to handle. The switches fused shut, and the heat stripped insulation from the wiring inside the tank. Nobody realized. The tank flew anyway, carrying damaged wires bathed in liquid oxygen.

About fifty-five hours into the flight, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the tanks, a routine step meant to keep the supercold contents evenly mixed. Swigert flipped the switch. Moments later there was a bang and the spacecraft shuddered. A spark from the exposed wires had ignited the insulation inside the tank, and the pressure rose until the tank tore open, damaging a panel on the side of the service module. Swigert radioed that they had a problem. Lovell repeated it, and the famous phrase, slightly altered from what was actually said, entered history.

At first the crew and the controllers on the ground thought they were looking at faulty instruments. But the warning lights told a worse story. Voltage was dropping. Oxygen pressure in the first tank was falling, and the second tank had already gone dark. Lovell looked out a window and saw gas streaming into space. The oxygen was the lifeblood of the ship, because it fed both the crew's breathing and the fuel cells that produced power and water. Within a couple of hours the command module would be dead. The Moon landing was gone, and the only question was whether the men could be brought home.

The flight director on duty, Gene Kranz, gathered his team and set one priority above all others. They had to get the crew back alive. The ship was roughly two hundred thousand miles from Earth, and its trajectory was a gentle arc that, if left alone, would loop around the far side of the Moon and slingshot back toward home. The problem was what to do with the three days in between, and how to stay alive inside a crippled machine.

The answer was to use the lunar module as a lifeboat. Aquarius had its own oxygen, batteries and engine, but it was designed to support two men for two days on the surface of the Moon, not three men for four days of travel. Lovell, Haise and Swigert crowded into the small cabin while Odyssey was shut down to save its precious batteries, which would be needed for the final return to Earth. Engineers worked out how to share the lunar module's limited supplies and told the crew to switch off nearly everything, including most of the heaters and the guidance computer.

Several hours after the explosion, as the ship swung around the Moon, the crew fired the lunar module's descent engine to speed up the trip home. Without the burn they would have reached Earth much later, with dwindling supplies. They set up the burn by hand, using the Earth itself as a guide in the window. Later, they made a smaller correction the same way, because the ship had drifted slightly and a steep or shallow angle at the atmosphere would have been fatal.

Life aboard became grim. The cabin grew so cold that water condensed on the walls and the men huddled in their flight suits, trying to sleep. Water was rationed to a few ounces a day, and Haise developed a fever from an infection. Most dangerous of all was the air. The lunar module's canisters, which absorb exhaled carbon dioxide, were designed for two men and were filling up. The command module had spare canisters, but they were square and the lunar module's sockets were round. On the ground, engineers gathered the same items the crew had aboard, including cardboard, plastic bags, hoses and duct tape, and built an adapter on a table. They read the instructions to the crew, who copied the design, and the carbon dioxide levels began to fall.

Meanwhile Ken Mattingly, the man who had been grounded, worked in a simulator on the ground for long hours. Powering up Odyssey after days of cold was something no one had ever done. The batteries had to last through reentry and the sequence had to be rewritten from scratch so as not to drain them. Mattingly and the engineers found a procedure that worked, and the crew received it in pages of careful dictation.

On the last day the crew returned to Odyssey and powered it up. Before reentry, they jettisoned the service module, and for the first time saw the damage. An entire panel had been blown off the side, and the interior looked scorched and ruined. Lovell described it to Houston with quiet disbelief. Finally they released Aquarius, the little ship that had carried them so far, and turned toward the atmosphere.

Reentry brings a period of radio silence, normally about three minutes, as the hot gas around the capsule blocks signals. On April 17 the silence stretched on longer than expected. Controllers watched the clock, and the room in Houston grew quiet. Nobody knew whether the heat shield had been damaged by the explosion. Then Swigert's voice came through, and the capsule appeared under three orange and white parachutes.

Odyssey splashed down in the Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship, the USS Iwo Jima. The crew were tired, thin, and dehydrated, but they were alive. The mission had lasted almost six days. It was called a successful failure, and the label stuck because the lessons were so large. Investigators redesigned the oxygen tanks and their wiring, and later missions flew safely.

More than the engineering, the story endures because of how people behaved when the plan fell apart. Controllers and astronauts, working with little sleep and no precedent, improvised with what they had. They never treated the crew's survival as someone else's problem. The Moon would be reached again, but Apollo 13 remains remembered as the flight where the goal was simply to come home.
